items.title: From neo-nazi to soccer coach for refugees | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>A former far-right extremist now coaches a soccer team of young refugees. As a coach and mentor, he helps them build a sense of community and settle into their new home.

Thomas Eichstätt, known to everyone as "Eichi,” used to be deeply involved in the far-right scene in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Today, he volunteers in the small town of Torgelow as the coach of FC Pio. 
Many of the young players he coaches have fled their home countries. They face an array of challenges in their adopted country: they must find jobs, navigate a lack of acceptance, and process their experiences as refugees.
But on the field, what matters most is the moment. Soccer offers these players structure and a sense of belonging. 
Off the field, many are caught up in the difficult process of integration and are consumed by a longing for home. Whether on the field or off of it, "Eichi” is there for them. For some players, he has become an important role model.
At the same time, the soccer coach is coming to terms with his own past. "I used to be a bad person,” says Eichstätt, of his time in the far-right scene. He receives no payment for his work with FC Pio—the financially strapped municipality can’t afford to fund his efforts.
Loraine Blumenthal’s film shows how soccer and personal commitment can build bridges—even in an environment characterized by frequent political demands for deportation.

items.title: Why Germany Stopped Working
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>If you’re looking to upgrade your business wardrobe, I can recommend giving Tailor Store a try. Their shirts are made to your measurements, so you can create something that fits both your body and your personal style. My viewers receive 25% off their first order through my link: https://www.tailorstore.com/patrickboyle

Germany just freed up half a trillion euros to rebuild itself — and eighteen months later, the money has barely moved. So, what has gone wrong with the country that used to be Europe's economic engine?

Everyone has a favourite villain: the end of cheap Russian gas, Chinese competition, Trump's tariffs. But none of them explains why a town outside Berlin can't spend two million euros to resurface a road, even after the cash has been handed over. In this video I look at the real problem underneath Germany's economic stall — a system so built around caution and consensus that it can't move, even when it desperately needs to.

We get into the suspended debt brake and the €500 billion that won't spend, the phantom construction sites, Germany's shift from mechanical engineering to a software-driven economy it wasn't built for, the "Export World Champion" trap, and why the American alternative — pouring billions into moonshots and space-based power grids — might be the opposite pathology rather than the answer. Featuring the work and ideas of Wolfgang Münchau (Kaput), Michael Pettis, Adam Tooze, and reporting from the Financial Times, the Wall Street Journal, and Bloomberg.

Is Germany's decline permanent, or is the recovery already quietly underway? That's the open question — and it's not really a German question. It's just that Germany got there first.

This documentary retraces the attacks of September 11th, 2001 in precise chronological order - in the air, at Ground Zero, in newsrooms and in the centers of power in the USA.  Archival footage, audio recordings and findings from the 9/11 Commission Report make it possible to reconstruct the events, almost in real time.

items.content:
<article>Airing just two days after 9/11, this documentary offered vital context on U.S. efforts to track Osama bin Laden, his terrorist network and his role in earlier attacks on Americans. (Aired 2001)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

In the hours after 9/11 — the worst terror attack on the U.S. in history — the CIA and FBI briefed political leaders in Washington, D.C. that their search for the terrorists responsible was focusing on one name above all others: Osama bin Laden. 

With opening and closing commentary from legendary journalist Bill Moyers, FRONTLINE’s “Hunting bin Laden,” which aired two days after the 9/11 attacks, captured the shock, grief and horror that gripped the U.S. when the twin towers fell — and documented the emergence of one central question: Why did U.S. intelligence agencies fail so tragically to “connect the dots” and uncover this enormous operation in time?

Built on an investigation into bin Laden and his militant Islamist network that FRONTLINE had aired two years earlier, and featuring new interviews conducted in the hours after 9/11, “Hunting bin Laden” was a collaboration with The New York Times. Director and producer Martin Smith and correspondent Lowell Bergman pieced together how bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi Arabian exile then believed to be hiding in Afghanistan, had eluded the U.S. while building a terror network and calling for the killing of Americans.

The documentary traced how the U.S. responded when bin Laden’s ideology emerged in connection with several major acts of Islamist terrorism against Americans in the 90s — from the 1993 attack on the World Trade Center, to the bombings of U.S. military installations in Saudi Arabia, to the 1998 bombings of U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania. It also raised tough questions about the evidence used to justify Washington’s retaliatory missile strikes in Sudan, a country where bin Laden was once based, following those embassy bombings. 

At the time “Hunting bin Laden” aired, the search for survivors in the wake of the 9/11 attacks was ongoing. As Moyers noted, a connection between bin Laden and the attacks had yet to be officially established.

“How do we bring the guilty to justice without making martyrs of them? And can we distinguish between those who commit the crimes and the innocent who share their culture but not their cause?” Moyers asked. “Not only our security as a nation is at stake, but our values as a people.”

items.title: Osteoarthritis - New hope for the knee | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Cold therapy, knee distraction or cartilage transplantation from the nose to the knee: what really helps with knee pain? New procedures are bringing fresh hope to people with osteoarthritis and joint degeneration.

Knee pain, wear and tear, osteoarthritis: millions of people suffer from these conditions. Natural remedies and high-tech medicine can alleviate the symptoms and improve joint mobility.  

Cartilage loss in the knee was long considered irreversible. The cartilage acts as a shock absorber between the bones of the joint and cushions the impact of each step. Once it starts wearing away, the bones rub against one another. This can lead to osteoarthritis; often accompanied by pain and restricted movement.

This is where an innovative approach from The Netherlands comes in: knee joint distraction. When the bones of the knee joint are pulled slightly apart, this creates a space that stimulates the body's natural cartilage-repair mechanisms. In Germany, orthopedic surgeon Kaywan Izadpanah from the University Medical Centre Freiburg is one of the first doctors to perform this procedure.

Researchers at Basel University Hospital are trying something else. They remove a small piece of tissue from the nasal septum of patients, cultivate the cells in the laboratory, and then transplant the cultured tissue into damaged areas of the knee joint. The procedure aims to repair cartilage damage and improve joint function.

For mild knee and joint pain, non-surgical remedies are an option. The "Rostock Seals” swear by the power of cold-water therapy: the swimming club’s members find renewed vitality through ice bathing in the wintery Baltic Sea. Some take it a step further, utilizing a cryotherapy chamber set at minus 110 degrees. They report immediate relief from their symptoms and an improved sense of well-being.

items.title: The chicken chasseur recipe alternative you did not know
items.author: French Cooking Academy
items.content:
<article>Today, we’re digging into Auguste Escoffier’s archives to make Chicken Ottero a stunning French classic and a close cousin to the famous Poulet Chasseur (Chicken Hunter). By substituting white wine with Port and deglazing with caramelized chicken juices, button mushrooms, and fresh tarragon, you get an amazingly deep, rich, and aromatic sauce.

Recipe: https://www.thefrenchcookingacademy.com/recipes/chickenottero

Ingredients for the Chicken:

1 Whole Chicken (broken down into 4 pieces: 2 breasts, 2 legs/thighs; save carcass & wings for stock)
20 g Unsalted Butter
1 tbsp Vegetable or Cooking Oil
Salt & freshly ground Black Pepper

Quick Tomato-Stock Base:
Chicken carcass & wing offcuts (chopped small)
1 tbsp Oil
Mirepoix (1 small Carrot, 1 small Onion, 1 Celery stalk, finely diced)
1 tbsp Tomato Paste
2 cups (500 ml) Store-bought Beef or Veal stock
Fresh Thyme & 1–2 Bay leaves
1 clove Garlic
Pinch of Black Pepper (and optional tiny pinch of Salt)

Sauce & Garnish:
100 ml Red Port Wine
1 Shallot, finely diced
150 grams Button Mushrooms (sliced)
1–2 tbsp Fresh Tarragon, leaves plucked & finely chopped
20 g Beurre Manié ( equal parts butter & flour, e.g., 10 g butter + 10 g flour mixed)
20 g Cold Unsalted Butter (for finishing/mounting the sauce)
Fresh parsley or tarragon (optional, for garnish)

11:03 – Straining & Thickening the Stock

18:06 – Taste Test & Final Thoughts
